I.M. Pei. The Chinese-American architect celebrated for geometric modernism and the elegant integration of buildings into urban landscapes, earning him the Pritzker Prize and making him a defining figure in late modernist architecture.

Pei lived from 1917 to 2019. His most iconic work is the Louvre Pyramid in Paris, completed in 1989. It's a glass and steel pyramid that modernized the entrance to the historic museum and was initially controversial but has become iconic. He created the Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong in 1989, a striking geometric glass structure with a lattice exterior that became the city's skyline symbol. He designed the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in Cleveland in 1995, a glass and steel building evoking both musical energy and architectural monumentality.

Pei was a pioneer of the geometric crystalline form, using triangles, hexagons, and tessellating shapes as both structural and aesthetic elements. He studied under Walter Gropius at Harvard, absorbing Bauhaus principles while developing his own minimalist, geometric language. He emphasized the relationship between building and urban context, designing structures that create public space and enhance their surroundings.

His National Center for Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colorado, completed in 1967, exemplifies his integration of structure into natural landscape through careful site planning. Pei was drawn to geometric minimalism much like Mies van der Rohe, sharing Mies's commitment to structural clarity through glass and steel. He was influenced by Le Corbusier's rationalism, though Pei softened it with sculptural geometry. As a direct apprentice of Walter Gropius, Pei absorbed Bauhaus philosophy and applied it to contemporary urbanism in his own distinctive way.
